subject: Creativity
title: How Songs Get Stuck: The Science of Earworms
description: A micro-lesson that makes How Songs Get Stuck: The Science of Earworms usable.

hook.text: Baby Shark, Twinkle Star, Bohemian Rhapsody — some songs loop in your head for hours. Your brain has been hijacked.

buildup.text: Earworms (involuntary musical imagery) affect 98% of people.

discovery.text: Research shows earworm songs share features: a common melodic contour with one unusual interval that grabs attention.

twist.text: The auditory cortex replays the song on a loop, trying to 'complete' it.

climax.text: Hit songwriters exploit this deliberately. Max Martin (Backstreet Boys, Taylor Swift) engineers melodic hooks designed.

punchline.text: Earworms aren't accidental. The catchiest songs are neuroscience experiments.

quiz.question: What musical features make a song more likely to become an earworm?
options: Simple melody with one unexpected interval

details.summary: Earworms are involuntary musical memories that loop in the mind. They exploit the brain's tendency to complete patterns. Songs with simple, repetitive melodies and unexpected rhythmic hooks are most likely to become stuck because they activate but never fully satisfy the pattern-completion drive.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding earworms reveals how memory, attention, and pattern recognition interact in the brain. For songwriters, the science of earworms provides insights into what makes melodies memorable and commercially successful.
takeaways: Earworms exploit the brain's compulsive need to complete patterns
Simple melodies with slight irregularities are most likely to stick
Over 90 percent of people experience earworms at least weekly

faq.question: How do you get rid of an earworm?
faq.answer: Research suggests engaging with a moderately challenging cognitive task, listening to the complete song, or replacing it with another song. The stuck loop occurs because the brain has unfinished acoustic business. Completing or replacing the pattern helps resolve it.

faq.question: Why are some songs more likely to become earworms?
faq.answer: Songs with simple, catchy melodies, moderate tempo, and a slight twist or irregularity in the pattern are most susceptible. The combination of predictability and surprise creates a loop the brain keeps trying to resolve.
